second_defensible.def: Another option is a reasonable, natural or plausible answer for a careful student.

source_underspecified.def: The line/passage leaves out what is needed, so several options fit some plausible filling ("all sort of possible").

key_wrong.def: The key is false: wrong agent (who does what), or it asserts an inference the source never makes.

factual_error.def: A real-world claim in the source (a sport's rule, a law, a named fact) is false.

self_contradiction.def: The source contradicts itself in dates, names, numbers, events or explanations.

unnatural_speech.def: A transcript reads as scripted: no contractions, stilted lines ("Let us do that"), unestablished speaker gender.

batch_pattern.def: Across items the key is predictable from a pattern: key order, punctuation only in keys, identical key prose, one template.

key_imprecise.def: Key is a narrower/looser/regional word or adds a detail, but no rival competes.

rival_some_pull.def: A rival has "some pull" from a gap or ambiguity, but the text still decides.

story_logic_gap.def: A story/transcript logic gap (who signs what; a notebook entry that reverses its purpose) that does not change the key.

distractor_too_easy.def: Distractors are far from the passage and easy to eliminate.

option_set_reused.def: The same distractor set (typically attitude words) is reused across passages.

difficulty_off.def: The item or answer is too easy/obvious overall.

skill_mislabel.def: The item tests a different skill than labelled (a purpose/inference item answerable as a detail).

key_stands_out.def: The key is the longest or the odd one out by form, category or wording.

option_wording.def: An option is ungrammatical, idiomatically odd, or copies the passage verbatim.

praise/none.def: No defect named (a lucky guess, praise).

entries.note: the transcript’s logic has a gap. the staff member says, “We match on language first and treat the subject as a preference.” If the subject were really just a preference, the student would have been matched with a Spanish speaker anyway, even without an engineer. Yet she wasn’t matched at all, and the staff member then offers to put her on the open list while keeping “the preference” on her record. The explanation contradicts itself: in practice, the subject was treated as a requirement. A careful listener might be confused about why the request stalled. A simple fix: “We hold a request until we can meet both parts, and this semester there was no engineer to give you.” That explains the delay and keeps the rest of the conversation intact. Like the bicycle conversation, this one avoids contractions, and here it’s even more noticeable: “Let us do that” sounds very unnatural; nobody says that in conversation. “You do not have to,” “you are matched,” “You will hear from a partner” add to the stiffness. Compare the conversations that use contractions naturally (“I’d like,” “don’t,” “you’re”). These two may have been produced differently, so check the full conversation set and apply contractions consistently.
entries.rationale: The transcript says subject is "a preference" yet treats it as a requirement — the explanation contradicts itself and a careful listener would be confused (REGISTER L260, v6-04). Also no contractions.

entries.note:
The transcript contradicts itself about winter gowns:

First: “The winter order closes in September and those gowns come from another supplier,” suggesting winter gowns are ordered.
Then: “And the winter one? — Rented on the day. We keep a stock of gowns in the hall,” meaning winter gowns aren’t ordered at all.
Then only the hood “has to be ordered.” But if “the winter order closes in September” and it’s now after September, can the hood still be ordered? The conversation doesn’t say.

A careful listener will be confused about whether winter gowns are ordered or rented and whether the deadline has passed. A clearer version: “The winter order is for hoods only, and it closes in September; the gowns are rented on the day from our own stock.” If it’s currently past September, the staff member should mention an exception for hoods.
entries.rationale: Winter gowns are first ordered (order closes in September) then rented on the day; the transcript contradicts itself and leaves the deadline unclear (REGISTER L260, v6-12).

entries.note:
The logic problem: Mr. Bello’s notebook records each caller’s name and “whatever they had mentioned.” The new entry has the nurse’s name at the top, but the details underneath are the narrator’s (biology class, cross-country), not anything the nurse said about herself. Read strictly, it reverses the notebook’s purpose. A careful reader might wonder what the entry is for: is it a reminder to ask the nurse about the narrator’s biology class next time?

The intended meaning, a symbolic handover, comes through, and B is still clearly the best answer. But the entry would make more sense if it recorded something the nurse shared, with the narrator’s details elsewhere. For example, have the nurse mention something of her own (“her son’s first semester away”), and Mr. Bello records that. Alternatively, keep the entry as is but make the gesture explicit, for example Mr. Bello saying, “Now she knows you. Next time, you ask her something.”
entries.rationale: The notebook entry records the narrator's details under the nurse's name, reversing the notebook's stated purpose; "B is still clearly the best answer". A story-logic flaw, not a contradiction of stated facts.

entries.note:
The rule problem, which matters a lot here: offside isn’t judged when a player kicks the ball. It’s judged when a teammate passes the ball to them. A player can’t be offside from his own dribble. Also, the reference point is the second-to-last opponent (usually the last outfield defender, since the goalkeeper counts), not simply “the last defender.” As written, the forward did nothing offside, so the narrator’s call, the coach’s “the call was right,” and this item’s key are all technically wrong.

This is worth fixing because:

Many students play soccer and will know the rule, so the passage loses credibility.
The narrator says they “had spent the week memorizing the rulebook,” which makes the error stand out.
The key teaches an incorrect rule.

A fix that keeps the story: “a Hornets forward took a pass from a teammate while standing behind the last Rockets defender.” The key would then read “was behind the last defender when a teammate passed to him.” (A note for accuracy: many leagues don’t enforce offside at under-10 at all, but it’s reasonable for this league to.)
entries.rationale: Offside is judged on a teammate's pass, not the forward's own kick, so the narrator's call and the key teach a wrong rule (REGISTER L235). Held from release.

entries.note: The precision issue: a queue usually means people standing and waiting their turn, often in British English. entries.note:
two things stand out:

No contractions. “I do not think I ever registered it,” “It is in the compound,” “the depot will not release anything,” “we did not cut one, because yours was not locked.” Every other conversation in the set uses contractions naturally (“I’d,” “don’t,” “you’re”). Without them, this one sounds stiff and scripted, which is a real problem for a listening item meant to model natural speech. I’d add contractions throughout (“I don’t think I ever registered it,” “It’s in the compound,” “won’t release,” “didn’t cut one”).
Speaker labels are reversed. In the other conversations, the student is A and the staff member is B; here the student is B and the officer is A, and B speaks first. It doesn’t affect the item, but if the app or audio script relies on consistent labels, it could cause confusion. Standardize them.
entries.rationale: Transcript has no contractions and reads as scripted; he calls it "a real problem for a listening item meant to model natural speech" — the listening material itself is defective even though the key is unique. Also reversed speaker labels (secondary, display).
